excerpts: This is a port of Microsoft's TRELLIS.2 — a state-of-the-art image-to-3D model — from CUDA-only to Apple Silicon via PyTorch MPS.
TRELLIS.2 depends on several CUDA-only libraries.
This port replaces each of them with a backend that runs on Apple Silicon:

|`flex_gemm` |`mtlgemm` (Pedro Naugusto's Metal port) with `backends/conv_none.py` fallback |Sparse 3D convolution. The Metal port is the default now; the pure-PyTorch gather-scatter path is the fallback for machines without the Metal Toolchain. |
|`o_voxel._C` hashmap |`backends/mesh_extract.py` |Mesh extraction from dual voxel grid (pure Python) |
|`flash_attn` |PyTorch SDPA |Scaled dot-product attention for sparse transformers (padded, not fused — room for improvement) |
|`cumesh` |Skipped during decode |Called on meshes large enough to crash the Metal port; replaced with `fast_simplification` before baking |
|`nvdiffrast` |`mtldiffrast` (Metal) with pure-Python fallback |Differentiable rasterization for texture baking |
Additionally, all hardcoded `.cuda()` calls throughout the codebase were patched to use the active device instead.

**Texture Baking** : By default we use the Metal stack released by [@pedronaugusto](https://github.com/pedronaugusto) — [`mtldiffrast`](https://github.com/pedronaugusto/mtldiffrast) , [`mtlbvh`](https://github.com/pedronaugusto/mtlbvh) , [`mtlmesh`](https://github.com/pedronaugusto/mtlmesh) , and his CPU fork of [`o_voxel`](https://github.com/pedronaugusto/trellis2-apple) — which exposes `o_voxel.postprocess.to_glb` .

If the Metal toolchain is unavailable, we fall back to `backends/texture_baker.py` : xatlas UV unwrap, then a scipy cKDTree + inverse-distance weighting over the sparse voxel grid at native 512 resolution.
macOS on Apple Silicon (M1 or later) Python 3.11+
24GB+ unified memory recommended (the 4B model is large) ~15GB disk space for model weights (downloaded on first run)
Run setup (creates venv, installs deps, clones & patches TRELLIS.2, builds Metal backends if the toolchain is available) bash setup.sh
To skip the Metal build (for example on older hardware or to speed up setup): ```shell SKIP_METAL=1 bash setup.sh ```
(Recommended) Download the Xcode Metal Toolchain so setup can build the Metal-accelerated texture baker. Without this, setup falls back to a pure Python KDTree baker (slower, slightly lower quality).
**Hole filling disabled** : Decode-time hole filling requires `cumesh` . The Metal port segfaults on decoder-sized meshes, so we skip this step. Output meshes may have small holes.

**Sparse attention is not fused** : The SDPA-padded wrapper works but is the single largest remaining bottleneck (~80 s of a 5m 13s run, the sparse structure sampling phase). A fused Metal attention kernel would be a meaningful perf win.

**Pre-simplified before texture bake** : The mesh is decimated from ~800K to ~200K faces before Metal BVH construction to avoid builder instability. If you need the full-resolution mesh, export it via the OBJ output (which is written before simplification).
**No training support** : Inference only.

Without it, `generate.py` falls back to `conv_none.py` for diffusion and monkey-patches `o_voxel.postprocess._grid_sample_3d` with a `torch.nn.functional.grid_sample` call for the bake. The fallback path works but is slower and leaves mild ring artifacts on curved surfaces.
Generates **400K+ vertex meshes with baked PBR textures** from a single image in **~5 minutes 13 seconds on M4 Pro** (24GB, cold start, weights cached, cool machine, pipeline type `512` ).
About 3m 20s of that is actual generation and baking; the remaining ~1m 45s is pipeline load that happens once per Python process.

|Pipeline load (first call per process) |103s | |Sparse structure sampling (12 steps) |80s | |Shape SLat sampling (12 steps) |22s | |Texture SLat sampling (12 steps) |12s | |Shape SLat decoder (VAE forward) |~20s |

The shape and texture decoder VAEs got 2.5–2.9× faster after [Pedro Naugusto fixed four bugs in `mtlgemm`](https://github.com/shivampkumar/trellis-mac/issues/1) (zero-copy MPS, real fp16/bf16 kernels, real masked implicit GEMM, no per-call `waitUntilCompleted` ). Before his fix, the decoder path was ~38s; now it's ~27s.
Memory usage peaks at around 18GB unified memory during generation.
First-ever run adds ~15GB of HuggingFace weight downloads (TRELLIS.2, DINOv3, RMBG-2.0) — network-bound, not included above.
With `SKIP_METAL=1` (pure-Python KDTree baker) the texture bake takes ~15s instead of ~11s and coverage near UV chart boundaries is slightly softer.
M4 Pro throttles aggressively under sustained load, and I've measured the same run taking 6–10× longer when the CPU had already been pinned for an hour before I started.

One thing that burned me during testing: after the M4 Pro had been doing heavy compute for a few hours, the same pipeline slowed from ~3.5 min generation to ~36 min purely from thermal throttling — nothing in the code path changed.

excerpts: This is a port of Microsoft's TRELLIS.2 — a state-of-the-art image-to-3D model — from CUDA-only to Apple Silicon via PyTorch MPS.
TRELLIS.2 depends on several CUDA-only libraries.
This port replaces each of them with a backend that runs on Apple Silicon:

|`flex_gemm` |`mtlgemm` (Pedro Naugusto's Metal port) with `backends/conv_none.py` fallback |Sparse 3D convolution. The Metal port is the default now; the pure-PyTorch gather-scatter path is the fallback for machines without the Metal Toolchain. |
|`o_voxel._C` hashmap |`backends/mesh_extract.py` |Mesh extraction from dual voxel grid (pure Python) |
|`flash_attn` |PyTorch SDPA |Scaled dot-product attention for sparse transformers (padded, not fused — room for improvement) |
|`cumesh` |Skipped during decode |Called on meshes large enough to crash the Metal port; replaced with `fast_simplification` before baking |
|`nvdiffrast` |`mtldiffrast` (Metal) with pure-Python fallback |Differentiable rasterization for texture baking |
Additionally, all hardcoded `.cuda()` calls throughout the codebase were patched to use the active device instead.

**Texture Baking** : By default we use the Metal stack released by [@pedronaugusto](https://github.com/pedronaugusto) — [`mtldiffrast`](https://github.com/pedronaugusto/mtldiffrast) , [`mtlbvh`](https://github.com/pedronaugusto/mtlbvh) , [`mtlmesh`](https://github.com/pedronaugusto/mtlmesh) , and his CPU fork of [`o_voxel`](https://github.com/pedronaugusto/trellis2-apple) — which exposes `o_voxel.postprocess.to_glb` .

If the Metal toolchain is unavailable, we fall back to `backends/texture_baker.py` : xatlas UV unwrap, then a scipy cKDTree + inverse-distance weighting over the sparse voxel grid at native 512 resolution.
macOS on Apple Silicon (M1 or later) Python 3.11+
24GB+ unified memory recommended (the 4B model is large) ~15GB disk space for model weights (downloaded on first run)
Run setup (creates venv, installs deps, clones & patches TRELLIS.2, builds Metal backends if the toolchain is available) bash setup.sh
To skip the Metal build (for example on older hardware or to speed up setup): ```shell SKIP_METAL=1 bash setup.sh ```
(Recommended) Download the Xcode Metal Toolchain so setup can build the Metal-accelerated texture baker. Without this, setup falls back to a pure Python KDTree baker (slower, slightly lower quality).
**Hole filling disabled** : Decode-time hole filling requires `cumesh` . The Metal port segfaults on decoder-sized meshes, so we skip this step. Output meshes may have small holes.

**Sparse attention is not fused** : The SDPA-padded wrapper works but is the single largest remaining bottleneck (~80 s of a 5m 13s run, the sparse structure sampling phase). A fused Metal attention kernel would be a meaningful perf win.

**Pre-simplified before texture bake** : The mesh is decimated from ~800K to ~200K faces before Metal BVH construction to avoid builder instability. If you need the full-resolution mesh, export it via the OBJ output (which is written before simplification).
**No training support** : Inference only.

Without it, `generate.py` falls back to `conv_none.py` for diffusion and monkey-patches `o_voxel.postprocess._grid_sample_3d` with a `torch.nn.functional.grid_sample` call for the bake. The fallback path works but is slower and leaves mild ring artifacts on curved surfaces.
Generates **400K+ vertex meshes with baked PBR textures** from a single image in **~5 minutes 13 seconds on M4 Pro** (24GB, cold start, weights cached, cool machine, pipeline type `512` ).
About 3m 20s of that is actual generation and baking; the remaining ~1m 45s is pipeline load that happens once per Python process.

|Pipeline load (first call per process) |103s | |Sparse structure sampling (12 steps) |80s | |Shape SLat sampling (12 steps) |22s | |Texture SLat sampling (12 steps) |12s | |Shape SLat decoder (VAE forward) |~20s |

The shape and texture decoder VAEs got 2.5–2.9× faster after [Pedro Naugusto fixed four bugs in `mtlgemm`](https://github.com/shivampkumar/trellis-mac/issues/1) (zero-copy MPS, real fp16/bf16 kernels, real masked implicit GEMM, no per-call `waitUntilCompleted` ). Before his fix, the decoder path was ~38s; now it's ~27s.
Memory usage peaks at around 18GB unified memory during generation.
First-ever run adds ~15GB of HuggingFace weight downloads (TRELLIS.2, DINOv3, RMBG-2.0) — network-bound, not included above.
With `SKIP_METAL=1` (pure-Python KDTree baker) the texture bake takes ~15s instead of ~11s and coverage near UV chart boundaries is slightly softer.
M4 Pro throttles aggressively under sustained load, and I've measured the same run taking 6–10× longer when the CPU had already been pinned for an hour before I started.

content.executive_answer:
On an Apple Silicon Mac, the practical ranking is:

1. **Best proven native port:** TRELLIS.2 through `shivampkumar/trellis-mac` using PyTorch MPS, or the newer `pedronaugusto/trellis2-apple` MLX/backend project.
2. **Best lightweight baseline:** TripoSR, but the official application does not select MPS automatically. It selects `cuda:0` or CPU, so MPS requires a small community code patch or compatible wrapper.
3. **Best Hunyuan route:** Hunyuan3D-2/2.1 through MLX ports, not the official CUDA-oriented Python pipelines. Hunyuan3D-2.5 has no comparably verified Apple port in the evidence reviewed.
4. **Officially possible but slow:** Stable Fast 3D has experimental MPS support and explicitly documents an M1 Max 64GB test, but an M1 Pro report measured roughly **7-9 minutes per generation**.
5. **Not presently a practical Mac target:** InstantMesh. Its official setup is CUDA 12.1 plus xformers, with no MPS or CPU instructions.

Apple Silicon can execute many neural-network operations through PyTorch MPS, but CUDA-dependent rasterizers, sparse voxel operators, mesh extractors, and fused attention kernels do not automatically translate to MPS. A working Mac port normally replaces those components rather than merely changing the device string.

content.what_specifically_breaks_on_apple_silico:
### TRELLIS/TRELLIS.2

For original TRELLIS, the CUDA-sensitive surface includes fused attention (`flash-attn`, with `xformers` as an alternative), differentiable rasterization (`nvdiffrast`), octree/rasterization (`diffoctreerast`), sparse convolution (`spconv`), mesh/splatting utilities, and Kaolin. [what_specifically_breaks_on_apple_silicon[0]] [8] The official repo requires Linux, NVIDIA hardware, and CUDA compilation. [what_specifically_breaks_on_apple_silicon[0]] [8]

TRELLIS.2 is more explicit: `flexgemm` is Triton-based sparse convolution, `o-voxel` handles the structured voxel representation, `cumesh` handles CUDA mesh postprocessing, `nvdiffrast` handles rendering, and `nvdiffrec` handles PBR rendering. [what_specifically_breaks_on_apple_silicon[1]] [10] The MPS fork's replacements are therefore meaningful: it does not pretend that MPS can load the CUDA binaries; it substitutes implementations for each one. [what_specifically_breaks_on_apple_silicon[2]] [12]

The MLX fork is a second route, but do not conflate it with the MPS port. Its repository says it adds an MLX backend and Metal postprocessing while preserving the original CUDA pipeline; the evidence does not enumerate every generation stage as MLX-native or provide an Apple benchmark. [what_specifically_breaks_on_apple_silicon[3]] [18]

### Hunyuan

Hunyuan's central portability problem is not the same as TRELLIS's. The verified blockers are the custom rasterizer and differentiable renderer used for painting. [what_specifically_breaks_on_apple_silicon[4]] [5] The Swift/MLX implementation avoids those CUDA builds by implementing shape and paint in MLX and Metal-compatible components. [what_specifically_breaks_on_apple_silicon[5]] [21]

The terms `torch-cluster`, `spconv`, `o_voxel`, and custom sparse voxel kernels should not be automatically assigned to Hunyuan. They are relevant to some 3D repositories, but the official Hunyuan evidence reviewed here specifically names `custom_rasterizer` and `DifferentiableRenderer`, not those other packages.

### InstantMesh, TripoSR, and SF3D

InstantMesh is the least documented for Mac: CUDA 12.1, xformers, CUDA device selection, and no fallback instructions. [what_specifically_breaks_on_apple_silicon[6]] [9] The official evidence does not establish an `nvdiffrast` import in the repository, although nvdiffrast is a CUDA-only rasterizer generally and appears in third-party deployment discussions. Do not treat a third-party dependency list as proof that every InstantMesh revision uses it.

TripoSR is smaller and more portable, but its official app's binary choice is CUDA or CPU, not CUDA/MPS/CPU. [what_specifically_breaks_on_apple_silicon[7]] [20] A Mac user therefore needs to patch device selection and test every downstream operation. Its `torchmcubes` troubleshooting confirms that CPU fallback exists, but not that MPS is supported. [what_specifically_breaks_on_apple_silicon[8]] [6]

SF3D is the most honest official Mac documentation: MPS is explicitly marked experimental, OpenMP is required, MPS may consume more memory than CUDA, and CPU can be forced. [what_specifically_breaks_on_apple_silicon[9]] [7]

content.docker_desktop_on_macos:
**Ordinary Docker Desktop Linux containers do not receive Apple Metal/MPS GPU passthrough.** Docker's official explanation is that Metal requires direct hardware access and that there is no Metal GPU passthrough for containers. [docker_desktop_on_macos[0]] [3]

Therefore, a normal Linux container running PyTorch cannot simply see the host's Apple GPU as `mps`. In practical terms, a Dockerized TRELLIS, Hunyuan, TripoSR, InstantMesh, or SF3D workflow on macOS should be assumed to run CPU-only unless it connects to a remote NVIDIA machine or uses a separately engineered host integration.

Docker Model Runner is a special case, not a counterexample. Docker packages a `vllm-metal` backend but runs the Metal stack natively on the macOS host; the container image supplies the software payload and communicates with a host-side server. [docker_desktop_on_macos[0]] [3] [docker_desktop_on_macos[0]] [3] This does not provide general Metal passthrough for arbitrary PyTorch MPS applications.
content.recommendation:
For an M-series Mac today, use **TRELLIS.2 MPS** if you need textured, high-quality assets and can tolerate minutes per asset. Use **Hunyuan3D Swift/MLX or Hunyuan3D-2.1 MLX** if you need Hunyuan's shape/paint pipeline and have enough unified memory. Use **TripoSR** when speed and simplicity matter, but patch device selection to MPS and validate the mesh extraction path. Use **Stable Fast 3D** only with the expectation that official MPS is experimental and may be very slow. Avoid spending time on **InstantMesh** or **Hunyuan3D-2.5** on Mac unless you are prepared to port CUDA components yourself or call a remote Linux/NVIDIA service.

The most important practical rule is: run these ports natively on macOS, not inside Docker Desktop, and treat every quoted runtime as hardware-, resolution-, quantization-, and cold-start-dependent.
